Smart Dimension (Sketch dimension)

Fusion's Smart Dimension (D): sets a size that DRIVES the shapes — type 25 and the line becomes 25 mm.

How to use

  1. A circle: click it, type the diameter.
  2. A line's length: click it, then anywhere empty.
  3. Two lines: the angle between them. Two points: their distance. A point and a line: the distance between them.
  4. Two points not level with each other: one more click places the number — above or below them for the HORIZONTAL distance, left or right for the VERTICAL, between them for the straight one.
  5. An arc's two ends, then the arc itself: its arc length.
  6. A point or line and a centerline, the number placed beyond the centerline: the diameter (Ø), as for a revolve.
  7. A face of the part (3D): the distance to that face.
  8. Shift+click a circle: to its near or far side instead of its centre.
  9. A value may be an expression of the variables (w / 2).

Tip: A dimension the sketch cannot take (it is fully defined) is added DRIVEN, in brackets: it only measures. Right-click a dimension to switch Driven; Delete constraint removes one.

Extruded Boss/Base (Linear extrude)

Turns a flat sketch shape into a solid by pushing it straight out of its plane — the usual way a part begins, and how a boss is added to one.

How to use

  1. Draw the shape in a sketch (Sketch Mode, then a plane or a flat face) — or select 2D shapes you already have: rectangle, circle, polygon, text, lines that close an area.
  2. Click Extruded Boss/Base. One closed shape is extruded at once; overlapping shapes show their regions in the 3D view — click the ones to keep, then Done or right-click. With no sketch left to extrude it asks for a face to sketch a boss on.
  3. Its window opens beside a blue arrow in the 3D view: drag the arrow or type the Distance; Direction is One side, Two sides or Symmetric; End condition is Blind or Through all; Reverse direction turns it round.
  4. OK or Enter keeps it; Cancel or Esc takes it back. Later, select the extrude: the arrow returns and Properties holds the same settings, with Twist and Scale (top) to shape it.

Tip: Only 2D shapes can go inside — a 3D object there turns red.
menu.status: Extruded Boss/Base (Linear extrude) — Turns a flat sketch shape into a solid by pushing it straight out of its plane — the usual way a part begins, and how a boss is added to one.

menu.tip:
Revolved Boss/Base (Rotate extrude (lathe))

Spins a 2D profile round the Z axis like a lathe — cups, flanges, bottles, wheels.

How to use

  1. Draw HALF the cross-section, to the right of the vertical axis (X ≥ 0): X becomes the radius, Y the height.
  2. Select it and click Revolved Boss/Base.
  3. Angle below 360 makes a partial revolve (a slice).

Tip: A profile crossing X = 0 turns red — keep it on one side.
menu.status: Revolved Boss/Base (Rotate extrude (lathe)) — Spins a 2D profile round the Z axis like a lathe — cups, flanges, bottles, wheels.

menu.tip:
Swept Boss/Base (Sweep along path)

Drives a flat 2D profile along a 3D path — pipes, handrails, cable runs, springs, chain links. Corners are mitred and the path can be smoothed into a curve.

How to use

  1. Draw the cross-section as 2D shapes (a circle for a pipe, a rectangle for a rail) around the origin: seen with the path coming towards you, x is right and y is up.
  2. Select it and click Swept Boss/Base.
  3. In Properties, type the Path points (X, Y, Z) the profile should follow; Smoothing rounds the corners into a curve.
  4. Wall thickness > 0 makes it hollow (a pipe); Closed loop joins the end to the start (an O-ring); Twist and Scale act over the length.

Tip: Only 2D shapes go inside. The result is baked into the program, so a sweep cannot sit inside a loop — put the loop inside the sweep instead.
menu.status: Swept Boss/Base (Sweep along path) — Drives a flat 2D profile along a 3D path — pipes, handrails, cable runs, springs, chain links. Corners are mitred and the path can be smoothed into a curve.

menu.tip:
Lofted Boss/Base (Loft through sections)

Joins a series of 2D shapes — one cross-section each — into one solid, keeping their corners as sharp edges: car bodies, boat hulls, bottles with flats, wings.

How to use

  1. Draw each cross-section as a polygon (or rectangle, circle) in the XY plane, around the same origin.
  2. Select them in order and click Lofted Boss/Base.
  3. In Properties, type one height (Z) per section, in the same order as the shapes in the tree.
  4. Smoothing adds curved in-between sections; the ones you drew stay exactly where they are.

Tip: Give every section the same number of points and they join point to point, so each corner runs as a crisp edge. Rotate the loft to make it run along X.
menu.status: Lofted Boss/Base (Loft through sections) — Joins a series of 2D shapes — one cross-section each — into one solid, keeping their corners as sharp edges: car bodies, boat hulls, bottles with flats, wings.

menu.tip:
Move Face (Push / pull faces)

Moves a flat face straight out (a boss, a taller wall) or in (a pocket, a recess), like SketchUp — with an optional inset that leaves a rim around it.

How to use

  1. Select the object(s) in the tree (Ctrl-click to add more), or click one in the 2D view. Pick the part.
  2. Click Push / pull, then click flat faces in the 3D view.
  3. Each face comes out 5 mm: set its Distance in Properties (negative cuts in) and its Inset (a rim).
  4. Esc when done; right-click ▸ Pick faces to add more.

Tip: Faces apply in order: click the top you just raised to raise it again.
menu.status: Move Face (Push / pull faces) — Moves a flat face straight out (a boss, a taller wall) or in (a pocket, a recess), like SketchUp — with an optional inset that leaves a rim around it.

menu.tip:
Fillet (Fillet edges (round / chamfer))

Rounds the edges you click — SolidWorks' Fillet. A convex edge is rounded off, an inside corner is filled in; Chamfer cuts a flat instead of a curve.

How to use

  1. Select the object(s) in the tree (Ctrl-click to add more), or click one in the 2D view. Pick the solid (or several).
  2. Click Fillet: the 3D view asks for edges.
  3. Click an edge to round it; one click on a cylinder's rim takes the whole rim, a click on a face rounds every edge round that face. Esc or right-click when done.
  4. Set the Radius (or the chamfer's setback) in Properties. Right-click the fillet ▸ Pick edges to add more.

Tip: The rounding shows in the exact OpenSCAD render (a moment after each change, or F5) — the quick preview cannot cut.
menu.status: Fillet (Fillet edges (round / chamfer)) — Rounds the edges you click — SolidWorks' Fillet. A convex edge is rounded off, an inside corner is filled in; Chamfer cuts a flat instead of a curve.

menu.tip:
Chamfer (Bevel edges)

Rounds or chamfers EVERY sharp edge of a part at once — outside edges, inside corners or both — with true rounded corners where three edges meet. The part keeps its size.

How to use

  1. Select the object(s) in the tree (Ctrl-click to add more), or click one in the 2D view. Pick the part.
  2. Click Chamfer.
  3. Width: the radius of the round (mm).
  4. Segments: steps across it (1 = a flat chamfer).
  5. Profile: 0.5 round, 0.25 flat, towards 1 squarer, lower a cove.
  6. Edges sharper than: leave gentle creases (a cylinder's facets) alone.

Tip: To round only some edges, use Fillet edges and click them.
menu.status: Chamfer (Bevel edges) — Rounds or chamfers EVERY sharp edge of a part at once — outside edges, inside corners or both — with true rounded corners where three edges meet. The part keeps its size.

menu.tip:
Full Round Fillet

Rounds a face right across: a half round tangent to the two faces either side — the top of a lug, a rib end, a tab (SolidWorks' Full round fillet). The radius is half the width, found by itself.

How to use

  1. Select the object(s) in the tree (Ctrl-click to add more), or click one in the 2D view. Pick the part.
  2. Click Full Round Fillet: its window opens beside the view.
  3. In the 3D view click a SIDE face, then the CENTRE face, then the other SIDE face.
  4. OK (or Esc) keeps it; Cancel takes it away.

Tip: Click nothing and the top face is rounded across its narrow way; click the centre face alone and its sides are found.
menu.status: Full Round Fillet — Rounds a face right across: a half round tangent to the two faces either side — the top of a lug, a rib end, a tab (SolidWorks' Full round fillet). The radius is half the width, found by itself.

menu.tip:
Draft

Tilts a part's side faces by a small angle about a neutral plane, so it comes out of a mould (SolidWorks' Draft): the part narrows going away from the bottom (or the top).

How to use

  1. Select the object(s) in the tree (Ctrl-click to add more), or click one in the 2D view. Pick the part.
  2. Click Draft: every side face leans in by 3°.
  3. In Properties set the Draft angle (°) and the Neutral plane (bottom: narrower at the top; top: narrower at the bottom).
  4. To draft only some faces, list a point on each in Faces to draft.

Tip: A negative angle leans the faces out instead. Caps stay flat and the solid stays closed.
menu.status: Draft — Tilts a part's side faces by a small angle about a neutral plane, so it comes out of a mould (SolidWorks' Draft): the part narrows going away from the bottom (or the top).

menu.tip:
Dome

Bulges a flat face out into a smooth dome (or dents it in) — a button top, a knob, a lid (SolidWorks' Dome). The face's edge stays where it is.

How to use

  1. Select the object(s) in the tree (Ctrl-click to add more), or click one in the 2D view. Pick the part.
  2. Click Dome: its window opens beside the view; the top face is domed 10 mm.
  3. Set the Height; tick Reverse to dent the face in instead.
  4. Click other flat faces in the 3D view to dome them instead; click one again to leave it.
  5. OK (or Esc) keeps it; Cancel takes the Dome away.

Tip: A round face becomes exactly half an ellipsoid.
menu.status: Dome — Bulges a flat face out into a smooth dome (or dents it in) — a button top, a knob, a lid (SolidWorks' Dome). The face's edge stays where it is.

menu.tip:
Wrap

Writes text or a flat sketch ROUND a cylinder, raised (Emboss) or cut in (Deboss) — a name on a mug, a scale on a knob (SolidWorks' Wrap).

How to use

  1. Select the object(s) in the tree (Ctrl-click to add more), or click one in the 2D view. Pick the round part.
  2. Click Wrap: its window opens beside the view with a text already wrapped across the front.
  3. Type the Text and its Size; choose Emboss or Deboss and the Depth.
  4. Turn it round the part with Start angle.
  5. For a shape instead of text, draw 2D shapes inside the Wrap (after the part): x runs round the cylinder, y up it.

Tip: The radius is the part's own; give Radius in Properties for a cylinder that is only part of the model.
menu.status: Wrap — Writes text or a flat sketch ROUND a cylinder, raised (Emboss) or cut in (Deboss) — a name on a mug, a scale on a knob (SolidWorks' Wrap).

menu.tip:
Deform (point / curve to curve)

SolidWorks' Deform. Point: pushes the body along an axis from a point — a dome from a flat grille (distance, radius, stiffness). Curve to curve: bends bodies from one curve onto another — a straight rod onto an S-shaped path; the initial curve's ends land on the target curve's ends.

How to use

  1. Point type: click the Origin row of the tree (or a face in 3D) for the point, choose the axis, type the Deform distance and radius, pick the Shape, then click the body and OK.
  2. Curve to curve: draw the target curve as a sketch (lines and fillet arcs) and keep the rod's centre line as a construction line.
  3. Click Deform: its window opens beside the view.
  4. In the tree click the sketch that holds the INITIAL curve, then the TARGET sketch, then the bodies to bend.
  5. OK makes the Deform; Cancel leaves everything as it was.

Tip: A body beyond the end of the curves carries on along the end tangent; where the two curves coincide the body does not move.
menu.status: Deform (point / curve to curve) — SolidWorks' Deform. Point: pushes the body along an axis from a point — a dome from a flat grille (distance, radius, stiffness). Curve to curve: bends bodies from one curve onto another — a straight rod onto an S-shaped path; the initial curve's ends land on the target curve's ends.

menu.tip:
Shell (Shell (hollow))

Turns a solid into a hollow Shell of even wall thickness — a cup, a case, a lid, a lighter print. One side can be left open.

How to use

  1. Select the object(s) in the tree (Ctrl-click to add more), or click one in the 2D view. Pick the solid to hollow.
  2. Click Shell: its window opens beside the view.
  3. Set the Thickness (mm).
  4. Click the faces to remove in the 3D view (the top of a cup); click one again to keep it. With no face the part is hollow but closed, so it looks the same from outside.
  5. OK (or Esc) keeps it; Cancel takes the Shell away.

Tip: A wall thicker than half the part's smallest dimension leaves no room for a cavity; the shell turns red and says so.
menu.status: Shell (Shell (hollow)) — Turns a solid into a hollow Shell of even wall thickness — a cup, a case, a lid, a lighter print. One side can be left open.

Render (cache as mesh)

OpenSCAD's render(): tells OpenSCAD to compute its contents as one finished mesh in its own preview. The shape is unchanged; a complex boolean inside a loop previews faster.

How to use

  1. Select the objects and click Render.
  2. Raise Convexity if OpenSCAD's preview shows see-through faces (the most walls a ray can cross, halved).

Tip: KherveCAD's own preview ignores it; it is kept so the program reads the same in OpenSCAD.

Grows the first child by the shape of the second — a box plus a small sphere is a box with every edge rounded.

How to use

  1. Select the body FIRST, then the shape to sweep round it (a small sphere for rounding).
  2. Click Minkowski.

Tip: To round only chosen edges use Fillet edges instead; this rounds all of them and is slow on big parts.
menu.status: Minkowski (sweep one shape round another) — Grows the first child by the shape of the second — a box plus a small sphere is a box with every edge rounded.

menu.tip: Deform & sculpt

Smooth blend

Melts shapes together like clay: where they meet, the seam becomes a smooth fillet instead of a sharp crease.

How to use

  1. Select the object(s) in the tree (Ctrl-click to add more), or click one in the 2D view. Use spheres, capsules, ellipsoids, boxes, rounded boxes or cylinders.
  2. Click Smooth blend.
  3. Blend radius sets how far the melting reaches; Detail sets the mesh resolution (higher = finer, slower).

Tip: A blend cannot sit inside a loop — the loop varies, the melted mesh cannot.

  2. Click Bend.
  3. Length axis = the long direction; Bend toward = which way it curls; Angle = the total bend.
  4. Max edge: smaller gives a smoother curve.

menu.tip:
Lattice (free-form)

Free-form reshaping: move the 8 corners of the bounding box and the shape follows smoothly — squash, lean or bulge it.

How to use

  1. Select the object(s) in the tree (Ctrl-click to add more), or click one in the 2D view.
  2. Click Lattice.
  3. In Properties, each row moves one corner by dX, dY, dZ (row order: X changes fastest, then Y, then Z).
menu.status: Lattice (free-form) — Free-form reshaping: move the 8 corners of the bounding box and the shape follows smoothly — squash, lean or bulge it.

menu.tip:
Subdivide (smooth)

Smooths a blocky shape by splitting and relaxing every triangle — boxes turn into pebbles.

How to use

  1. Select the object(s) in the tree (Ctrl-click to add more), or click one in the 2D view.
  2. Click Subdivide.
  3. Levels 1–4: each level makes it smoother (and 4× heavier).
  4. Keep edges sharper than: 30–60° keeps a part's real edges crisp (a cylinder's rims, a box's corners) while its curved sides round off — 0 rounds everything.
menu.status: Subdivide (smooth) — Smooths a blocky shape by splitting and relaxing every triangle — boxes turn into pebbles.

menu.tip:
Decimate (fewer triangles)

Makes a heavy part light: fewer triangles, the same shape — a scan, a sculpt, a threaded part or a tree that slows the view or the export. Flat areas lose triangles first, detail last.

How to use

  1. Select the object(s) in the tree (Ctrl-click to add more), or click one in the 2D view. Pick the heavy solid.
  2. Click Decimate.
  3. Keep: the fraction of triangles to keep (0.25 = a quarter).
  4. Or within: a distance in mm the surface may move instead — 0.05 is invisible on a print.

Tip: A closed solid stays closed, so it still prints.
menu.status: Decimate (fewer triangles) — Makes a heavy part light: fewer triangles, the same shape — a scan, a sculpt, a threaded part or a tree that slows the view or the export. Flat areas lose triangles first, detail last.

menu.tip:
Remesh (clean solid)

Rebuilds a messy part as ONE clean closed solid of even triangles: overlapping pieces merge, inner walls and small holes in a scan disappear. Use it when a part will not print, bevel, shrinkwrap or cut.

How to use

  1. Select the object(s) in the tree (Ctrl-click to add more), or click one in the 2D view. Pick the messy part.
  2. Click Remesh.
  3. Voxel size: the detail kept (mm) — smaller is finer and heavier.
  4. Snap keeps the original surface exactly where it was.

Tip: Follow it with Decimate if the result is heavier than needed.
menu.status: Remesh (clean solid) — Rebuilds a messy part as ONE clean closed solid of even triangles: overlapping pieces merge, inner walls and small holes in a scan disappear. Use it when a part will not print, bevel, shrinkwrap or cut.

menu.tip:
Wireframe (struts)

Turns a part's edges into round printable struts with balls at the corners — lamp shades, cages, geodesic domes, lightweight lattices, wire sculptures.

How to use

  1. Select the object(s) in the tree (Ctrl-click to add more), or click one in the 2D view. Pick the part whose edges become struts.
  2. Click Wireframe.
  3. Strut thickness (mm) and sides (6 is round enough).
  4. Skip edges flatter than: 1° drops the diagonals of flat faces; 0 keeps every triangle edge.

Tip: Put a Decimate or Remesh inside it to choose the pattern.
menu.status: Wireframe (struts) — Turns a part's edges into round printable struts with balls at the corners — lamp shades, cages, geodesic domes, lightweight lattices, wire sculptures.

menu.tip:
Shell (Shell (hollow))

Turns a solid into a hollow Shell of even wall thickness — a cup, a case, a lid, a lighter print. One side can be left open.

How to use

  1. Select the object(s) in the tree (Ctrl-click to add more), or click one in the 2D view. Pick the solid to hollow.
  2. Click Shell: its window opens beside the view.
  3. Set the Thickness (mm).
  4. Click the faces to remove in the 3D view (the top of a cup); click one again to keep it. With no face the part is hollow but closed, so it looks the same from outside.
  5. OK (or Esc) keeps it; Cancel takes the Shell away.

Tip: A wall thicker than half the part's smallest dimension leaves no room for a cavity; the shell turns red and says so.
menu.status: Shell (Shell (hollow)) — Turns a solid into a hollow Shell of even wall thickness — a cup, a case, a lid, a lighter print. One side can be left open.

menu.tip:
Sculpt (brush strokes)

Pushes the surface about with a brush — Blender's sculpt mode: grab, inflate, smooth, flatten, pinch, and the creature brushes — snake hook (horns, tentacles, spikes), draw, clay strips, layer, elastic grab, pose (bend a limb) and mask.

How to use

  1. Select the object(s) in the tree (Ctrl-click to add more), or click one in the 2D view. (a blend, a subdivided cage or an imported scan works best).
  2. Click Sculpt: the panel opens and the brush is on the 3D view.
  3. Pick the brush, radius and strength, then DRAG over the surface: dabs follow the mouse. Grab, elastic grab and snake hook pull where you drag — a snake hook dragged off the surface pulls a horn out into the air.
  4. Crease and Ridge draw a line along the drag — a wrinkle, a vein, a tendon, a scar. Pose: click the joint, then drag the limb round it. Mask freezes what it covers.
  5. Shift while dragging smooths; [ and ] change the size; a press off the model still orbits. Strokes are kept in Properties: edit or delete any of them later. Skin roughness (Properties) adds pores and lumps over the whole surface.

Tip: Mirror repeats each stroke across the part's middle, so one horn makes two. Add Weathering on top and every crease darkens by itself.
menu.status: Sculpt (brush strokes) — Pushes the surface about with a brush — Blender's sculpt mode: grab, inflate, smooth, flatten, pinch, and the creature brushes — snake hook (horns, tentacles, spikes), draw, clay strips, layer, elastic grab, pose (bend a limb) and mask.

menu.tip:
Displace (scales, cracks, warts)

Gives a surface real skin: every vertex moves along its normal by a pattern — round scales, overlapping shingles, cracks, warts, chitin plates, ridged wrinkles, lumpy noise or a greyscale picture. Like Blender's Displace modifier.

How to use

  1. Select the object(s) in the tree (Ctrl-click to add more), or click one in the 2D view. (a sculpt, a blend, a body).
  2. Click Displace, then pick the pattern in Properties.
  3. Pattern size is how big one scale or wart is; height how far it stands out (negative carves it in — cracks).
  4. Within keeps it to a region (a belly, a back), fading out at the edges; Shingles overlap towards the axis you choose.

Tip: The surface is refined first to an eighth of the pattern size; set Refine to edge coarser if the part gets slow.
menu.status: Displace (scales, cracks, warts) — Gives a surface real skin: every vertex moves along its normal by a pattern — round scales, overlapping shingles, cracks, warts, chitin plates, ridged wrinkles, lumpy noise or a greyscale picture. Like Blender's Displace modifier.

menu.tip:
Shrinkwrap (onto a surface)

Presses one shape onto another: a garment, a cap, a strap or a decal hugs the body under it instead of floating a guessed distance off it — and follows it after a pose or a sculpt.

How to use

  1. Select the object(s) in the tree (Ctrl-click to add more), or click one in the 2D view. Select the piece to wrap FIRST, then the target (Ctrl+click).
  2. Click Shrinkwrap.
  3. Move each vertex: nearest (the closest point of the target) or project (along its normal, or an axis).
  4. Which vertices move: outside (only those inside the target — clothes), all (onto the surface) or inside.
  5. Offset: how far off the surface it sits (mm).

Tip: Blocky piece? Set Refine to split it first, so it can bend.
menu.status: Shrinkwrap (onto a surface) — Presses one shape onto another: a garment, a cap, a strap or a decal hugs the body under it instead of floating a guessed distance off it — and follows it after a pose or a sculpt.

menu.tip: Move & transform

Move/Copy Bodies (Translate (move))

Moves the selection by X, Y and Z millimetres.

How to use

  1. Select the object(s) in the tree (Ctrl-click to add more), or click one in the 2D view.
  2. Click Move/Copy Bodies.
  3. Type the X/Y/Z offsets.

Tip: Primitives already have their own X/Y/Z, and dragging in the 2D view moves too — Translate is for moving a whole group.
menu.status: Move/Copy Bodies (Translate (move)) — Moves the selection by X, Y and Z millimetres.

menu.tip:
Rotate Bodies (Rotate)

Turns the selection about X, then Y, then Z (degrees), around the origin (0, 0, 0).

How to use

  1. Select the object(s) in the tree (Ctrl-click to add more), or click one in the 2D view.
  2. Click Rotate Bodies.
  3. Type the angles.

Tip: It turns around the origin, so a part already moved away swings round: rotate first, then move.
menu.status: Rotate Bodies (Rotate) — Turns the selection about X, then Y, then Z (degrees), around the origin (0, 0, 0).

menu.tip:
Scale (Scale)

Multiplies the selection's size along X, Y and Z (1 = unchanged, 2 = double, 0.5 = half).

How to use

  1. Select the object(s) in the tree (Ctrl-click to add more), or click one in the 2D view.
  2. Click Scale.
  3. Type the factors.
menu.status: Scale (Scale) — Multiplies the selection's size along X, Y and Z (1 = unchanged, 2 = double, 0.5 = half).

menu.tip:
Mirror (Mirror)

Adds a Mirror image of features or bodies about a plane, the original kept: the copy follows every edit of it.

How to use

  1. Click Mirror — its window opens beside the view.
  2. Features / bodies to Mirror: click their rows in the tree (History) or the parts in the 3D view (the tree's selection is taken at once).
  3. Mirror plane / face: click Front, Top or Right Plane at the top of the tree or in the 3D view, a reference plane in the tree, or a flat face of the part.
  4. OK makes it; Cancel or Esc leaves nothing.

Tip: Front / Top / Right are the part's own planes, wherever the feature sits; the plane is in the Mirror's Properties after.
menu.status: Mirror (Mirror) — Adds a Mirror image of features or bodies about a plane, the original kept: the copy follows every edit of it.

menu.tip:
Resize (absolute size)

Scales what it holds to a size in millimetres rather than by a factor — OpenSCAD's resize(). Make a part exactly 40 mm long without working out the scale.

How to use

  1. Select the objects and click Resize.
  2. Type the new size along X, Y and/or Z; 0 keeps that axis.
  3. Tick Auto on an axis left at 0 to scale it with the others, keeping the proportions.

Tip: OpenSCAD scales about the origin, like scale(): centre the part first if it should grow evenly.
menu.status: Resize (absolute size) — Scales what it holds to a size in millimetres rather than by a factor — OpenSCAD's resize(). Make a part exactly 40 mm long without working out the scale.

menu.tip:
Matrix transform (multmatrix)

Applies a 4 x 4 affine matrix — the general transform that translate, rotate, scale, mirror and shear are all cases of. Every .csg file OpenSCAD writes places its shapes this way.

How to use

  1. Select the objects and click Matrix transform.
  2. Edit the rows: the first three columns turn, scale and shear; the fourth column moves (X, Y, Z).
  3. Leave the last row 0, 0, 0, 1.

Tip: Put a number off the diagonal (row 1, column 2) for a shear — something no other transform can do.
menu.status: Matrix transform (multmatrix) — Applies a 4 x 4 affine matrix — the general transform that translate, rotate, scale, mirror and shear are all cases of. Every .csg file OpenSCAD writes places its shapes this way.

menu.tip:
Mirror (Mirror)

Adds a Mirror image of features or bodies about a plane, the original kept: the copy follows every edit of it.

How to use

  1. Click Mirror — its window opens beside the view.
  2. Features / bodies to Mirror: click their rows in the tree (History) or the parts in the 3D view (the tree's selection is taken at once).
  3. Mirror plane / face: click Front, Top or Right Plane at the top of the tree or in the 3D view, a reference plane in the tree, or a flat face of the part.
  4. OK makes it; Cancel or Esc leaves nothing.

Tip: Front / Top / Right are the part's own planes, wherever the feature sits; the plane is in the Mirror's Properties after.
menu.status: Mirror (Mirror) — Adds a Mirror image of features or bodies about a plane, the original kept: the copy follows every edit of it.

menu.tip:
Linear / Circular Pattern (Pattern (linear / polar / grid))

Repeats its contents as copies — in a row, round an axis, or on a grid — like Blender's Array or a SolidWorks Linear / Circular Pattern. A bolt circle, a row of holes, a spiral stair, a peg board.

How to use

  1. Select what to repeat and click Linear / Circular Pattern (or click with nothing selected and drag objects into the empty Linear / Circular Pattern).
  2. Choose the Kind: linear (Count copies at Step X/Y/Z), polar (Count copies turned about the Axis over Angle°) or grid (Count X/Y/Z at Step X/Y/Z).
  3. Polar: Angle 360 spreads the copies evenly round the circle; below 360 they span the angle, first at 0°, last at Angle. Rise per copy lifts each one along the axis — a helix.

Tip: Every field takes an expression, so a pattern inside a loop can read the loop variable. Capped at 1000 copies.
menu.status: Linear / Circular Pattern (Pattern (linear / polar / grid)) — Repeats its contents as copies — in a row, round an axis, or on a grid — like Blender's Array or a SolidWorks Linear / Circular Pattern. A bolt circle, a row of holes, a spiral stair, a peg board.

menu.tip:
Scatter on surface

Copies one piece over a surface — spikes down a spine, warts, scales, barnacles, rows of teeth, eye clusters, rivets. Like Blender's particles: each copy stands along the surface normal, sized and turned a little at random.

How to use

  1. Model the piece at the origin standing up along +Z, base at z = 0 (a cone for a spike).
  2. Select the piece, then the body (Ctrl+click), and click Scatter: the first child is the piece, the rest the surface.
  3. In Properties: how many copies and how far apart, size and its variation, random spin and lean, sink into the surface, only faces looking one way, or a region.
  4. Mode Path puts the copies evenly along points you give — a spine, a jaw line — each dropped onto the surface; Taper makes them smaller towards the ends.

Tip: Edit the piece and every copy follows. Sink a little so no gap shows under a copy on a curved body.
menu.status: Scatter on surface — Copies one piece over a surface — spikes down a spine, warts, scales, barnacles, rows of teeth, eye clusters, rivets. Like Blender's particles: each copy stands along the surface normal, sized and turned a little at random.

menu.tip:
Gear (involute)

A true involute gear by module, tooth count and pressure angle — spur, helical, herringbone, internal (ring), rack, bevel or worm — with bore, backlash and root clearance. Two gears of the same module and pressure angle mesh at a centre distance of m (z1 + z2) / 2.

How to use

  1. Insert ▸ Mechanical features ▸ Gear.
  2. Choose the Kind, then the Module (tooth size) and Teeth.
  3. Set Thickness, a Bore, and for a helical or herringbone gear the Helix angle; a bevel gear needs its mate's tooth count.
  4. Print-in-place pairs want 0.1–0.2 mm of Backlash.

Tip: Every field takes an expression, so teeth = ratio * 10 keeps a pair in step; the code is kcad_gear(...), real OpenSCAD.
menu.status: Gear (involute) — A true involute gear by module, tooth count and pressure angle — spur, helical, herringbone, internal (ring), rack, bevel or worm — with bore, backlash and root clearance. Two gears of the same module and pressure angle mesh at a centre distance of m (z1 + z2) / 2.

menu.tip:
Thread (Thread (screw thread))

A real helical screw Thread — ISO metric, trapezoidal, square, buttress, tapered pipe or bottle neck — male, or as the slightly larger tap you subtract to make a nut or a threaded hole. Any number of starts, right or left hand.

How to use

  1. Insert ▸ Mechanical features ▸ Thread.
  2. Set the Profile, Major diameter, Pitch and Length (M8: 8 mm, 1.25).
  3. For a nut or a threaded hole tick Internal and put the Thread inside a Difference with the part; 0.2 mm Clearance prints well.

Tip: A thread is a twisted cross-section, so it previews exactly and renders fast — no boolean inside.
menu.status: Thread (Thread (screw thread)) — A real helical screw Thread — ISO metric, trapezoidal, square, buttress, tapered pipe or bottle neck — male, or as the slightly larger tap you subtract to make a nut or a threaded hole. Any number of starts, right or left hand.

menu.tip:
Hole (Hole (counterbore, countersink, nut trap…))

The solid to cut for a fastener: plain, counterbore, countersink, nut trap, heat-set insert, slot, or a teardrop that prints horizontally without support. Its top sits at z = 0 and it goes down, so it drops onto a face.

How to use

  1. Insert ▸ Mechanical features ▸ Hole.
  2. Pick the Kind and the sizes (M3: 3.2 mm Hole, 6 mm head).
  3. Move it onto the face, then select it with the part and click Difference.

Tip: Extends above the face keeps the cut clean on a flush face; the teardrop runs along X with its point up.
menu.status: Hole (Hole (counterbore, countersink, nut trap…)) — The solid to cut for a fastener: plain, counterbore, countersink, nut trap, heat-set insert, slot, or a teardrop that prints horizontally without support. Its top sits at z = 0 and it goes down, so it drops onto a face.

menu.tip:
Knurled cylinder

A cylinder covered in diamond knurling — two sets of helical grooves crossing — for a knob or a thumb screw you can grip.

How to use

  1. Insert ▸ Mechanical features ▸ Knurled cylinder.
  2. Set the Outer diameter and Length, how many Diamonds round and the Groove depth (0.6–1 mm prints well).

Tip: Put it in a Group with the knob's other shapes; the helix angle sets how tall the diamonds are.
menu.status: Knurled cylinder — A cylinder covered in diamond knurling — two sets of helical grooves crossing — for a knob or a thumb screw you can grip.

menu.tip:
Textured cylinder / panel

A cylinder or a flat panel with a relief pattern on its surface — ribs, waves, diamonds, bricks, hexagons, dimples or checkers — for grips, lids, lithophane-like panels and decoration.

How to use

  1. Insert ▸ Mechanical features ▸ Textured cylinder / panel.
  2. Choose the Shape and the Pattern, then its size (Pattern size) and how deep it goes (Relief depth).
  3. Raise Samples per pattern for a smoother relief.

Tip: Round a cylinder the pattern size is adjusted so it closes without a seam.
menu.status: Textured cylinder / panel — A cylinder or a flat panel with a relief pattern on its surface — ribs, waves, diamonds, bricks, hexagons, dimples or checkers — for grips, lids, lithophane-like panels and decoration.

menu.tip:
Base Flange/Tab

The flat sheet every sheet metal part starts from. With a sketch shape selected (rectangle, polygon, circle) the sheet takes that outline; with nothing selected it is 100 × 60 mm.

How to use

  1. Optional: draw the outline in a sketch and select it.
  2. Click Base Flange/Tab — a 2 mm sheet appears and stays selected.
  3. In Properties set the Thickness, Bend radius and K-factor (or apply a rule with Sheet Metal Rules).
  4. Go on with Edge Flange, Hem or Fold.

Tip: Unfold shows the flat blank at any time.
menu.status: Base Flange/Tab — The flat sheet every sheet metal part starts from. With a sketch shape selected (rectangle, polygon, circle) the sheet takes that outline; with nothing selected it is 100 × 60 mm.

menu.tip:
Arch Plate

A new base flange shaped like an arch — a half circle over straight sides: the back plate of a bracket.

How to use

  1. Click Arch Plate (nothing needs selecting).
  2. Give the Width (the arch's diameter), the straight height below the arch centre, the Thickness, Bend radius and K-factor.
  3. OK: the plate stands on the XY plane with its centre at the origin; Edge Flange comes next.

Tip: Any other outline: draw a polygon and use Base Flange/Tab.
menu.status: Arch Plate — A new base flange shaped like an arch — a half circle over straight sides: the back plate of a bracket.

menu.tip:
Convert to Sheet Metal

Turns a plate you already have — a thin cube or a sketch shape extruded to the sheet's thickness — into a sheet metal body, in the same place, so it can take flanges and unfold.

How to use

  1. Select the plate in the tree.
  2. Click Convert to Sheet Metal.
  3. Its thinnest side becomes the thickness; the status bar says what it found.

Tip: A cube standing on edge is converted standing on edge.
menu.status: Convert to Sheet Metal — Turns a plate you already have — a thin cube or a sketch shape extruded to the sheet's thickness — into a sheet metal body, in the same place, so it can take flanges and unfold.

menu.tip:
Edge Flange

Bends a wall up (or down) from an edge of the sheet, with the bend radius and allowance worked out for you.

How to use

  1. Select the sheet metal body (the only one in view is taken by itself).
  2. Click Edge Flange, then click the edge in the 3D view — Esc lets you choose it from a list instead.
  3. In the window set the Height (to the outside), the Angle (90 = square; negative bends down), the Bend radius and, to stop short of the corners, the two Insets.
  4. OK: the wall is added and the status bar gives the new flat blank size.

Tip: A flange's own outer edge can take another flange — that is how a box lip is made.
menu.status: Edge Flange — Bends a wall up (or down) from an edge of the sheet, with the bend radius and allowance worked out for you.

menu.tip:
Fold

Bends the flat sheet along a line across it (SolidWorks' Sketched Bend). The outline stays the flat blank; the bend allowance is centred on the line.

How to use

  1. Select the sheet metal body while it is still flat.
  2. Click Fold.
  3. Give the bend line by its two ends (X, Y on the sheet — it starts as a line across the middle), the Angle and the Bend radius.
  4. OK.

Tip: Fold BEFORE adding flanges or hems: a fold changes the edges they sit on, and is refused afterwards.
menu.status: Fold — Bends the flat sheet along a line across it (SolidWorks' Sketched Bend). The outline stays the flat blank; the bend allowance is centred on the line.

menu.tip:
Jog

Two opposite bends from one line (SolidWorks' Jog): the side you click stays fixed, the other side steps up (or down) by the offset through a sloped web and ends parallel to the first. The flat blank grows by the web.

How to use

  1. Select the sheet metal body, click Jog.
  2. Click two points on the sheet for the bend line (a nearly straight line is made straight); the line's ends can be typed.
  3. Click the side of the sheet that stays fixed (Fixed face).
  4. Set the Offset and its Dimension position (outside, inside offset, total), the Jog position, the Angle and the direction; the jog follows each change.
  5. OK.

Tip: Jog position says where the line falls: bend centre line, material inside / outside (its virtual sharps) or bend outside (the bends start on the line).
menu.status: Jog — Two opposite bends from one line (SolidWorks' Jog): the side you click stays fixed, the other side steps up (or down) by the offset through a sloped web and ends parallel to the first. The flat blank grows by the web.

menu.tip:
Hole

Cuts round holes in the flat plate; they follow their panel through a jog and show in the flat pattern and the DXF.

How to use

  1. Select the sheet metal body, click Hole.
  2. Set the Diameter, then click the sheet where each hole goes (0.5 mm grid).
  3. OK.

Tip: Change the Diameter after a click to resize the last hole.
menu.status: Hole — Cuts round holes in the flat plate; they follow their panel through a jog and show in the flat pattern and the DXF.

menu.tip:
Slot

Cuts a round-ended slot along a centre line you click.

How to use

  1. Select the sheet metal body, click Slot.
  2. Set the Width, click the slot's two ends.
  3. OK.

Tip: Slots follow their panel through a jog like holes.
menu.status: Slot — Cuts a round-ended slot along a centre line you click.

menu.tip:
Hem

Folds an edge right back over itself — a safe, stiff, rounded edge — leaving the rule's hem gap inside.

How to use

  1. Select the sheet metal body.
  2. Click Hem, then click the edge in the 3D view.
  3. Set the Length of the folded-back strip; tick Fold under to turn it down instead of over.
  4. OK.

Tip: The hem gap comes from the body's rule (Sheet Metal Rules).
menu.status: Hem — Folds an edge right back over itself — a safe, stiff, rounded edge — leaving the rule's hem gap inside.

menu.tip:
Path Flange

Several flanges in a row off one edge, a bend at every corner — a Z, a return lip, a channel — typed as length, angle pairs.

How to use

  1. Select the sheet metal body.
  2. Click Path Flange, then click the edge.
  3. Type the segments as “length, angle; length, angle”: 20, 90; 10, 90 goes up 20 then turns in 10.
  4. OK.

Tip: A negative angle bends the other way: 20, 90; 10, -90 is a Z.
menu.status: Path Flange — Several flanges in a row off one edge, a bend at every corner — a Z, a return lip, a channel — typed as length, angle pairs.

menu.tip:
Contour Flange

A NEW sheet metal body from an open profile seen from the side — a channel, a Z or a hat section — with one bend at every corner, stretched to a width.

How to use

  1. Click Contour Flange (nothing needs selecting).
  2. Type the profile's points as “X, Z; X, Z; …” in order: 0, 30; 0, 0; 50, 0; 50, 30 is a U channel 50 wide, 30 high.
  3. Set the Width (how long the section runs).
  4. OK: the body is made and can take edge flanges and hems.

Tip: Keep the corners square to start; the bend radius rounds them.
menu.status: Contour Flange — A NEW sheet metal body from an open profile seen from the side — a channel, a Z or a hat section — with one bend at every corner, stretched to a width.

menu.tip:
Mirror

Copies chosen features — an ear with its hole, tabs, holes, jogs — to the other side of a plane across the sheet.

How to use

  1. Select the sheet metal body.
  2. Click Mirror and tick the features to mirror.
  3. Choose the Mirror plane (across X or across Y) and its position.
  4. OK: the copies are added.

Tip: The copies are ordinary rows: edit or remove each on its own.
menu.status: Mirror — Copies chosen features — an ear with its hole, tabs, holes, jogs — to the other side of a plane across the sheet.

menu.tip:
Linear Pattern

Repeats chosen features at a fixed step — a row of gussets, holes or tabs.

How to use

  1. Select the sheet metal body.
  2. Click Linear Pattern and tick the features.
  3. Give the number of Instances (the original counts) and the Step; a gusset steps along its bend.
  4. OK.

Tip: A gusset 10 mm from the corner, 3 instances 30 apart, gives ribs at -30, 0 and 30 on an 80 mm flange.
menu.status: Linear Pattern — Repeats chosen features at a fixed step — a row of gussets, holes or tabs.

menu.tip:
Circular Pattern

Repeats chosen features round a centre — four tabs and their jogs round an opening.

How to use

  1. Select the sheet metal body.
  2. Click Circular Pattern and tick the features (a tab and its jog).
  3. Give the Instances, the Centre and the Angle (360 = a full turn, equally spaced).
  4. OK.

Tip: Tick the tab AND its jog so every copy is jogged too.
menu.status: Circular Pattern — Repeats chosen features round a centre — four tabs and their jogs round an opening.

menu.tip:
Sheet Metal Gusset

A stamped rib across the inside corner of a bend — stiffens a flange without extra parts.

How to use

  1. Select the sheet metal body.
  2. Click Sheet Metal Gusset, then click the bend in the 3D view.
  3. Give the Offset along the bend, the depths d1 / d2 up each face, the Width and the side Draft.
  4. OK: the rib is added (the flat pattern is unchanged).

Tip: Repeat it, or use a Linear Pattern, for a row of ribs.
menu.status: Sheet Metal Gusset — A stamped rib across the inside corner of a bend — stiffens a flange without extra parts.

menu.tip:
Jog Tab

Two bends along a line step the part beyond it out of the sheet's plane — a tab raised clear of the plate.

How to use

  1. Select the sheet metal body.
  2. Click Jog Tab, then click the line's start and end across the tab in the 3D view.
  3. Give the Jog offset and angle (negative = down) and the Bend radius; the line is stretched across the whole tab.
  4. OK: the end of the tab moves, the rest stays.

Tip: The line must cross only what moves: a tab, not the plate.
menu.status: Jog Tab — Two bends along a line step the part beyond it out of the sheet's plane — a tab raised clear of the plate.

menu.tip:
Tab

Merges a new tab — a strip with a round end and a hole — into the sheet, even inside an opening of it (a mounting lug).

How to use

  1. Select the sheet metal body.
  2. Click Tab.
  3. Give the Round end centre (U, V), the Width, the Length measured from that centre and the Direction (90 = up).
  4. Hole diameter 0 leaves the end solid. OK.

Tip: The tab's root must overlap the sheet: it is merged, not bent.
menu.status: Tab — Merges a new tab — a strip with a round end and a hole — into the sheet, even inside an opening of it (a mounting lug).

menu.tip:
Break Corner

Rounds (or chamfers) a sharp corner of the sheet — the flange's free corners, a plate's corners — in the part, the flat pattern and the DXF.

How to use

  1. Select the sheet metal body.
  2. Click Break Corner, then click near the corner in the 3D view.
  3. Give the Radius (tick Chamfer for a straight cut).
  4. OK: the corner is rounded.

Tip: Only convex corners with sides longer than the radius can be broken.
menu.status: Break Corner — Rounds (or chamfers) a sharp corner of the sheet — the flange's free corners, a plate's corners — in the part, the flat pattern and the DXF.

menu.tip:
Panel Hole

A round hole through the sheet — cut in the folded part, the flat pattern and the DXF.

How to use

  1. Select the sheet metal body.
  2. Click Panel Hole, then click the face where it goes.
  3. Check the Position (U, V in that panel) and give the Hole diameter.
  4. OK: the hole is cut; Unfold shows it on the blank.

Tip: A hole belongs to one panel (the base or one flange): keep it on that panel, clear of the bends.
menu.status: Panel Hole — A round hole through the sheet — cut in the folded part, the flat pattern and the DXF.

menu.tip:
Perforate

A field of round holes over the flat sheet, kept clear of the edges and the bends — in the part, the flat pattern and the DXF.

How to use

  1. Select the sheet metal body.
  2. Click Perforate.
  3. Set the Hole diameter, the Pitch (centre to centre — more than the diameter), the Margin and Staggered or Square.
  4. OK: the status bar counts the holes; Unfold shows them on the blank.

Tip: Run it again to change the field: it replaces the last one.
menu.status: Perforate — A field of round holes over the flat sheet, kept clear of the edges and the bends — in the part, the flat pattern and the DXF.

menu.tip:
Create Flat Pattern

Puts a flat copy of the body beside it: the blank to cut, with its bend lines, while the folded part stays as it is.

How to use

  1. Select the sheet metal body.
  2. Click Create Flat Pattern.
  3. The status bar gives the blank's size and the number of bends.

Tip: For the cutting file use Export Flat Pattern as DXF.
menu.status: Create Flat Pattern — Puts a flat copy of the body beside it: the blank to cut, with its bend lines, while the folded part stays as it is.

menu.tip:
Unfold

Shows the selected body flat — every bend opened out — to check the blank and its holes.

How to use

  1. Select the sheet metal body.
  2. Click Unfold.
  3. Click Refold to fold it back up.

Tip: Nothing is lost: it is the same body, shown flat.
menu.status: Unfold — Shows the selected body flat — every bend opened out — to check the blank and its holes.

menu.tip:
Refold

Folds an unfolded body back up to its bent shape.

How to use

  1. Select the unfolded sheet metal body.
  2. Click Refold.
menu.status: Refold — Folds an unfolded body back up to its bent shape.

menu.tip:
Sheet Metal Rules

Named sets of thickness, bend radius, K-factor and hem gap — “Steel 2 mm”, “Aluminium 1.5 mm”. A body given a rule follows it: change the rule and every such body changes.

How to use

  1. Click Sheet Metal Rules.
  2. New… adds a rule; select one to edit its four values.
  3. With a sheet metal body selected, apply the rule to it.
  4. Close.

Tip: The rules are document variables, so they are saved with the file and written into the OpenSCAD program.
menu.status: Sheet Metal Rules — Named sets of thickness, bend radius, K-factor and hem gap — “Steel 2 mm”, “Aluminium 1.5 mm”. A body given a rule follows it: change the rule and every such body changes.

menu.tip:

Writes the flat blank for a laser or punch: CUT outlines and holes, BEND_UP and BEND_DOWN lines and ETCH notes on their own layers, in millimetres.

How to use

  1. Select the sheet metal body.
  2. Click Export Flat Pattern as DXF.
  3. Choose where to save the file.

Tip: Send the bend table with it so the folder knows each angle.
menu.status: Export Flat Pattern as DXF — Writes the flat blank for a laser or punch: CUT outlines and holes, BEND_UP and BEND_DOWN lines and ETCH notes on their own layers, in millimetres.

menu.tip:
Export Bend Table

Every bend as a CSV table: direction, angle, radius, length, allowance and where its centre line lies on the flat blank.

How to use

  1. Select the sheet metal body.
  2. Click Export Bend Table.
  3. Choose where to save the file; open it in any spreadsheet.
menu.status: Export Bend Table — Every bend as a CSV table: direction, angle, radius, length, allowance and where its centre line lies on the flat blank.

  2. Click a face, a plane (Front / Top / Right in the tree or the 3D view), an edge or a corner: up to three references.

  1. Click a plane or a flat face.

How to use

  1. Click a face or edge.
  2. Click another.
  3. Esc ends.

Tip: Parallel faces also give the face-to-face distance.

menu.tip:
Surface from curves

An exact surface made from 3D curves — Rhino's Loft, Sweep, Sweep along two rails, Patch, Revolve and Extrude. Open surfaces are thickened into a solid you can print; STEP export keeps the exact surface.

How to use

  1. Draw the curves (Insert ▸ Draw 3D Curve), or add 3D curves.
  2. Select them in the tree, in order — Ctrl+click for several.
  3. Tools ▸ Surface from Curves (or right-click) and pick the kind.
  4. Change Make, Wall thickness, Ruled and the rest in Properties; editing a curve inside it reshapes the surface.

Tip: For a sweep the FIRST curve is the rail; for a patch the first is the closed boundary.

SubD (smooth cage)

A smooth surface shaped by a coarse cage — Rhino's SubD. Eight cage points make a pebble; a few dozen make a shoe, a car body, a head.

How to use

  1. Insert ▸ SubD Box, or select a solid and Tools ▸ Convert to SubD.
  2. Press Tab over the 3D view: Edit Mode opens the CAGE. Drag points, E extrudes a face, the surface follows.
  3. Smoothness, crease angle and creased edges are in Properties.

Tip: Tick Show the cage too to see it while you work outside Edit Mode.

Cuts surfaces where they cross and removes the pieces you click. Standard: the first surface is trimmed by the others; Mutual: every surface trims every other.

  2. Click Trim Surface and choose Standard or Mutual.
  3. Click each piece to REMOVE in the 3D view (click again to bring it back; Keep selections keeps them instead).

  1. Select the surface in the tree.

menu.tip:
3D Sketch (Draw 3D curve)  Ctrl+Alt+C

Click points in the 3D view to draw a smooth curve through them. Points SNAP to corners, the middle of edges, edges and surfaces — the marker says which — or land on the ground grid in empty space.

How to use

  1. Insert ▸ 3D Sketch, or Ctrl+Alt+C.
  2. Click each point. Hold Shift to go straight up or down from the last point; hold Alt to switch snapping off.
  3. Or just type a point — 10, 20, 5 — or @0, 0, 15 for 15 above the last one, then Enter.
  4. Enter, right-click or double-click finishes; Backspace takes a point back; C (or clicking the first point) closes a loop.

Tip: Dragging still turns the view, so you can look round between clicks.
menu.status: 3D Sketch (Draw 3D curve) — Click points in the 3D view to draw a smooth curve through them. Points SNAP to corners, the middle of edges, edges and surfaces — the marker says which — or land on the ground grid in empty space.

menu.tip:
3D Sketch Curve (3D curve)

A smooth (or straight) line through points in space, drawn as a round wire — a cable, a handrail, a bent rod, a coil, the rail for a sweep. Exported to STEP as an exact B-spline pipe.

How to use

  1. Insert ▸ Shapes & patterns ▸ 3D Sketch Curve.
  2. Edit the Points table: one row per point it passes through (X, Y, Z). Add rows to add bends.
  3. Pick Smooth or Straight, tick Closed loop for a ring, and set the Wire thickness.
  4. Right-click ▸ Make a Sweep Along This Curve to give it any profile.

Tip: Thin it right down and hide it to keep it as a guide.
